title: 'I Was Extremely Shocked': Rajinikanth Breaks His Silence on Vijay Becoming Tamil Nadu's Chief Minister
excerpt: The Superstar called it a matter of pride, dismissed jealousy rumours, and defended his friendship with MK Stalin — all in one press conference that Tamil diaspora couldn't stop replaying.
body:
For a week after Vijay was sworn in as Tamil Nadu's 17th Chief Minister on May 10, Rajinikanth said nothing. The silence was deafening. Here was the man who had once launched his own political party — who had spent decades as the unspoken king of Tamil Nadu's celebrity-political complex — watching a younger star achieve what he never did. Social media filled the vacuum with speculation: was it jealousy? Hurt? Indifference?

Then, at a press conference in Chennai this week, Rajinikanth spoke.

## "Shocked" and "Extremely Happy"

"I was extremely shocked," the 75-year-old actor told reporters, choosing his words with the precision of a man who has navigated Tamil Nadu's political minefields for decades. "And I was extremely happy."

The duality was telling. Rajinikanth acknowledged that Vijay's victory — **TVK winning 108 seats** and ending a near six-decade oscillation between DMK and AIADMK — was something nobody had truly believed was possible. Not even, apparently, Rajinikanth himself.

"What Vijay has achieved is historic," he said. "It goes beyond MGR. It goes beyond NTR. He did it independently, with his own party, in his first election. That's never happened before."

## Swatting Down the Jealousy Narrative

The press conference's most significant moments came when Rajinikanth addressed the jealousy rumours head-on. He had recently visited former Chief Minister MK Stalin at his residence — a courtesy call, he said, to a friend who had just lost power. Tamil media interpreted it as a political signal. Some commentators suggested Rajinikanth was aligning with the defeated DMK out of bitterness.

Rajinikanth wasn't having it.

"Stalin and I have a relationship that goes back years. There's a 28-year age gap between Vijay and me — we're from completely different generations. The idea that I'd be jealous of a young man's success... it's baseless."

He pointed out that he had congratulated Vijay immediately after the election results and that his political retirement — announced years ago after his party failed to gain traction — was final. "I have no political ambitions. Zero. I'm happy making films."

## Why the Tamil Diaspora Cares So Much

In Toronto, London, Singapore, and the Bay Area — wherever the Tamil diaspora gathers — the Rajinikanth-Vijay dynamic is practically a cultural Rorschach test. Rajinikanth is the god of an older generation: the man who defined what a Tamil superstar could be, whose films were events, whose political tease in the early 2000s sent the state into a frenzy. Vijay is the hero of the millennials and Gen Z Tamils: the action star who channeled middle-class frustration into a political movement that actually won.

Rajinikanth's endorsement — however measured — matters because it signals generational continuity rather than rivalry. For NRIs who grew up worshipping "Thalaivar" and now find themselves cheering for "Thalapathy," the press conference was permission to hold both loyalties without conflict.

## Kamal Haasan Weighs In

A day after Rajinikanth's presser, Kamal Haasan added his voice. "CM Vijay is a matter of pride," the actor-politician said, praising the new Chief Minister's early actions — including the closure of 717 government liquor outlets, a campaign promise that had been dismissed as populist pandering during the election.

Kamal's tone was markedly warmer than Rajinikanth's, perhaps because he carries less political baggage. Having run his own unsuccessful party, Makkal Needhi Maiam, he understands both the ambition and the difficulty of the celebrity-to-politician transition. His praise felt less strategic and more genuine.

## What Comes Next

Vijay has been Chief Minister for exactly one week. The liquor outlet closures have earned goodwill. His cabinet is a mix of party loyalists and technocrats. The real tests — water scarcity, industrial policy, the always-fraught relationship with the Centre — are months away.

But the Rajinikanth press conference closed a symbolic chapter. Tamil Nadu's three biggest screen icons — Rajinikanth, Kamal Haasan, and Vijay — are now aligned, however loosely, behind the idea that a film star can govern. Whether Vijay actually can remains to be seen. But the old guard has, at the very least, cleared the stage.
